author: Javier Bedía Prado
title: Argentina: reforma de extranjerización de tierras retrocedió, plan de desalojos sumarios fue aprobado
content:
En portada: Marcha contra propuesta de reforma a Ley de Tierras en Argentina.

Las movilizaciones masivas en Argentina obligaron al Gobierno de Javier Milei a retroceder en los puntos más cuestionados de su reforma a la Ley de Tierras. La presión en las calles de Buenas Aires y varias localidades del país hizo que el Ejecutivo retire del proyecto de Ley de inviolabilidad de la propiedad privada los capítulos de cuasi derogación de la Ley de Tierras y el que modificaba la Ley de manejo del fuego.

Sin embargo, el pasado miércoles 6 de agosto la Cámara de Senadores aprobó la propuesta con los apartados de desalojos en tierras rurales y urbanas, y de impedimentos a las expropiaciones públicas, los que generan resistencia por parte de los movimientos sociales.

Según la administración ultraderechista de Milei, los objetivos centrales del proyecto son eliminar restricciones que “limitan el derecho a la propiedad” y fortalecer la seguridad jurídica para atraer inversiones. En ese sentido, pretende anular el tope del territorio nacional que se puede vender a extranjeros, establecido en 15%. Actualmente trece millones de hectáreas del suelo argentino pertenecen a empresas foráneas, de acuerdo al Observatorio de Tierras.

Por su parte, el intento de modificación de la Ley de manejo del fuego apuntaba a eliminar el plazo de 60 años de prohibición para cambiar el uso del suelo tras un incendio, sea ocasionado o accidental, en bosques, áreas naturales protegidas y humedales, así como la traba por 30 años para realizar actividades agropecuarias y proyectos inmobiliarios.

“Con las modificaciones propuestas, la tierra se convierte en un activo financiero, disponible para capitales concentrados -muchos de ellos extranjeros-, en lugar de ser considerada un bien común al servicio de la producción. Este plan de concentración y extranjerización de la tierra consolida un modelo que prioriza la especulación por sobre la soberanía alimentaria. La tierra no es una mercancía más: es un bien finito cuyo control define qué se produce, cómo se produce y para quién”, manifiesta la Mesa Agroalimentaria Argentina.

A su vez, el Observatorio de Tierras, del Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas (Conicet) y la Universidad de Buenos Aires, considera la propuesta como “una contrarreforma a favor del capital”.

La Ley de Tierras, promulgada en 2011, fijó en 15% el límite de tierras rurales disponible para compañías y empresarios de otros países. Asimismo, establece un máximo de 1,000 hectáreas en la zona núcleo -las más productivas- de actividad agropecuaria para el mismo titular. La norma denomina extranjeras a las firmas controladas por hasta el 25% de personas jurídicas o físicas foráneas. En la gestión de Mauricio Macri se subió la participación a más del 51%.

La Cámara de Diputados decidirá la aprobación del proyecto de norma que busca profundizar las desigualdades en torno a la propiedad privada. El contenido más crítico es el capítulo que plantea juicios sumarios en casos de desalojos en zonas rurales o urbanas por usurpación u ocupación ilegal. La iniciativa desprotege a comunidades que no poseen títulos, al encarecer y judicializar los procesos de regularización, además de permitir desahucios sin sentencia firme y con la intervención de fuerzas estatales.

De esta forma, el gobierno planea acortar a 72 horas el plazo de ejecución de desalojos. En un contexto en que 80% de la superficie argentina productiva se encuentra en condiciones de arriendo, y entre el 60% y 70% de agricultores familiares es arrendatario.

“Este proyecto de ley profundiza un desequilibrio estructural porque otorga más poder a quienes poseen la tierra, pero no la trabajan, en detrimento de quienes producimos alimentos. Esto agravará situaciones de desalojos y precariedad”, observa la Mesa Agroalimentaria Argentina.

De otro lado, se intenta limitar la capacidad del Estado de expropiar bienes de utilidad pública, redefiniendo este criterio con prohibiciones más rígidas. Los arrendatarios de terrenos resultarían más afectados al aumentar los costos de procesos de expropiación e introducir el lucro cesante -la ganancia que dejaría de recibir el propietario- en la indemnización acordada. Esto complica el acceso a la tierra para los pequeños agricultores.

De acuerdo al Censo Nacional Agropecuario, el 1% de las unidades agropecuarias acapara el 36% de la tierra, mientras que el 55% de productores trabaja solo en el 2% de la tierra.

Entre otras medidas …

author: Rizomatica
title: Comunicado de amigos, familiares, lov y comunidades de los Presos Políticos Mapuche de Caso Grollmus de la Franja Lavkenche
content:
«COMUNICADO PÚBLICO


Lavken mapu, Pukem 2026.


Mari mari kom pu che, pu ke lov, pu ke mapu, eymun kom!

Tras reunirnos en txawün el día de hoy queremos dirigirinos a nuestro pueblo, a la opinión pública nacional e internacional, a la ocupación chilena en nuestro territorio.

19 de nuestros hermanos, compañeros, padre e hijos se encuentra ad portas de terminar su juicio oral, imputados todos por su supuesta participación en el atentado al Molino Grollmus. Lo vamos a decir de forma clara y sin metáforas, nuestros presos políticos son víctimas de la necesidad ansiosa del ministerio público por dar resultados al sistema político y a los colonos que ocupan nuestro territorio. Ellos no estan presos por ser delincuentes, sino, porque la unica forma que ha encontrado la ocupación para detener la justa y legitima lucha por el territorio y autonomía de los mapuche ha sido la persecución, los allanamientos, los desalojos, la prisión. Nuestros presos se encuentran en esa condición pues todos ellos se organizaron a lo largo y ancho de nuestro territorio para luchar por la recuperación de sus tierras, por levantar sus ngillatun, por dar dignidad a su gente.

El fiscal de la causa se encuentra con una querella en su contra por prevaricacion, los colonos Grollmus se juntaron directamente con el presidente Jose Kast, y el Ministro Arrau a definido públicamente este juicio como «trascendental para Chile». Durante el transcurso de las audiencias ha quedado en plena evidencia que el unico insumo de fiscalia es la declaración de personas sin nombre y rostro, nada más.

La situación es clara, nuestros hermanos, dignos y perseguidos, arriegan cadena perpetua solo por la inmesa presión del poder político para su encarcelamiento.

Hoy son los alegatos de clausura y declaramos que nuestros esfuerzos seran inclaudicables en búsqueda de justicia.


Amigos, familiares, lov y comunidades de los Presos Políticos Mapuche de Caso Grollmus de la Franja Lavkenche.»


*Enviado a la radio


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Gatillo fácil en Ituzaingó: Pidieron que se eleve a juicio la causa por la muerte de Juan Cruz Leal
content:
La fiscal María Alejandra Bonini solicitó la elevación a juicio de la causa por la muerte de Juan Cruz Leal y el intento de homicidio de su amigo Daniel Khune. En marzo el agente de Policía de la Ciudad Lucas Gómez les disparó cuando circulaban en su moto a un partido de fútbol. Desde la Unidad Funcional de Instrucción N° 2 Descentralizada en Ituzaingó consideraron que lo ocurrido debe ser calificado como  homicidio agravado. La Comisión por la Memoria es parte del proceso como particular damnificado institucional en su calidad de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura. El organismo alertó en su Informe Anual 2026, recientemente presentado, que el año pasado creció la violencia letal policial en la provincia de Buenos Aires, pasando de 135 casos en 2024 a 141 en 2025, la cifra mas alta de los últimos 10 años.


El policía acusado, Lucas Adrián Gómez, ya se encuentra con prisión preventiva ya que por su accionar y por otros antecedentes de violencia la medida había quedado ratificada por la Cámara de Apelación y Garantías de Morón. Ahora desde la Unidad Funcional de Instrucción N° 2 Descentralizada en Ituzaingó, María Alejandra Bonnini solicitó la elevación a juicio del caso calificando los delitos cometidos por Gómez como homicidio agravado por ser cometido por un miembro de fuerza de seguridad pública y por la utilización de un arma de fuego, en concurso real con homicidio agravado por ser cometido por un miembro de fuerza de seguridad pública y por la utilización de un arma de fuego en grado de tentativa.


En la elevación a juicio la fiscal describe que Gómez “con el claro designio de darles muerte y abusando de su función como miembro integrante de la fuerza policial, con pleno dominio y control de la fuerza, sin mediar palabra”, disparó con su arma de fuego reglamentaria contra Juan Cruz y su amigo. Ambos recibieron disparos, Juan Cruz no sobrevivió. El crimen ocurrió a principios de marzo una noche en que Juan Cruz Leal iba en moto con su amigo a jugar al fútbol cuando se cruzó con el Policía de la Ciudad que estaba de franco y de civil pero armado y les disparó porque imaginó que podían ser ladrones. Diez meses antes de la muerte de Juan Cruz, Gómez había disparado y matado a otro joven en el marco de un presunto intento de robo.


En el pedido de elevación y a partir del material probatorio la fiscal concluyó que en este caso Gómez “actuó de manera irreflexiva, atentando contra la vida humana cuando debió en su condición de policía anteponer la preservación de ese bien jurídico por sobre todo” y que “está claro que la situación que dio origen al accionar de Gómez no facultaba en modo alguno al imputado a esgrimir su arma de fuego y menos aún a disparar”.  En su declaración testimonial durante la instrucción el imputado dejó constancia de que, de llegar a juicio, iba a solicitar que fuera ante un jurado popular.


El policía ya había sido responsable de otro episodio de uso letal de la fuerza en mayo de 2025; de civil y fuera de servicio, Gómez asesinó a un joven que presuntamente intentó robarle la moto, le disparó al menos 5 veces por la espalda. Esa causa sin embargo no avanzó y el policía siguió en funciones; diez meses después, asesinó a Juan Cruz.


La Comisión Provincial por la Memoria interviene como particular damnificado institucional en su calidad de Mecanismo Local de Prevención de la Tortura y representa también a Daniel, el joven que sobrevivió al ataque.


Con relación a los casos de letalidad policial, el organismo relevó en su Informe Anual 2026 que crecieron las muertes en PBA: ascendieron a 141 personas (100 de ellas menores de 30 años), contra 135 del 2024. Del total, 90 fueron cometidas por miembros de la Policía Bonaerense, 25 de la Policía de la Ciudad, 19 de la Policía Federal, 4 de la Gendarmería Nacional y 3 de la Prefectura Nacional. La mayoría -87 casos- fueron cometidos por agentes en actividad pero fuera de servicio o de franco, defendiendo bienes propios, lo que visibiliza nuevamente la necesidad de derogar el estado policial.


El Informe hace un análisis en 60 de estas causas judiciales seleccionadas aleatoriamente, mostrando la desproporción en el uso de la fuerza letal. Los policías reconocen haber disparado al menos 195 veces, contra 12 disparos realizados por los atacantes, que en ningún caso impactaron en los agentes policiales. 195  contra 12. Y de los 195 disparos policiales, 116 impactaron en los supuestos atacantes ingresando por la espalda cuando la persona huía …

author: Jéssica Ribeiro
title: Como a caça conservadora ao voto feminino alimenta a violência contra a mulher
content:
Investigamos o que importa para os brasileiros além do que passa na campanha eleitoral. Leia mais reportagens como essa clicando

aqui

.


Maioria entre o eleitorado brasileiro, as mulheres estão no centro de uma ofensiva que cresce nas redes sociais. Falas disfarçadas de opinião política questionam o espaço feminino na vida pública e se misturam a ataques de ódio envolvendo desqualificações, ameaças ou associações a contextos de violência sexual – justamente no período em que a participação delas nas urnas se torna decisiva.


O

voto feminino

 foi reconhecido no Brasil pelo Código Eleitoral de 1932. Antes disso, propostas de participação de mulheres na política enfrentaram resistência e argumentos de que elas

não teriam a mesma capacidade intelectual

 dos homens.

Quase cem anos depois, a discussão mudou de linguagem e plataforma, mas não desapareceu e encontra eco em várias partes do mundo.


Na primeira semana de julho deste ano, um vídeo da influenciadora bolsonarista Pietra Bertolazzi ganhou projeção em todo o país por mostrá-la se juntando a uma campanha contra o voto feminino. “Sou contra”, disse, ao se referir ao voto de mulheres, bem como ao feminismo. O movimento espelha manifestações entoadas pela extrema direita em outros países, em especial, nos Estados Unidos.


Print do vídeo da influenciadora bolsonarista Pietra Bertolazzi


No dia 21 do mesmo mês, o influenciador bolsonarista Paulo Figueiredo retomou declaração feita por Jair Bolsonaro contra a deputada Maria do Rosário (PT-RS) em 2014, quando disse que

não estupraria Maria do Rosário

 porque ela “não merecia”, em referência à aparência da parlamentar. Figueiredo classificou como “genialidade” a fala de Bolsonaro e utilizou o episódio para atacar novamente a deputada, bem como a parlamentar Jandira Feghali (PCdoB-RJ).


O caso chegou à esfera judicial. Em agosto, a desembargadora do Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Rio Grande do Sul (TRE-RS), Vânia Heck, classificou a manifestação como misógina e determinou que o Google removesse trechos da transmissão por propaganda eleitoral antecipada

 negativa contra Maria do Rosário. Na decisão, a magistrada afirmou que as referências a Jandira Feghali não eram de competência da Corte gaúcha.


O link mencionado na ação foi retirado do ar. No entanto, cortes que replicam as falas de Figueiredo continuam disponíveis no canal do próprio influenciador. Procurado, o Google respondeu que a empresa cumpriu integralmente a decisão judicial.


“O YouTube é uma plataforma aberta, comprometida com a liberdade de expressão, com a integridade do debate público e atua em conformidade com a legislação. Agimos prontamente ao sermos notificados sobre violações à lei local, avaliando e processando ordens judiciais e notificações que atendam aos requisitos legais”, disse.


O episódio envolvendo Figueiredo expôs, ainda, outra camada do discurso contra a participação feminina na política. Em uma segunda transmissão analisada pela Justiça, o influenciador afirmou que mulheres “votam estatisticamente muito mal”, especialmente “as solteiras”. Nesse caso, a magistrada reconheceu a presença de “linguagem grosseira, sexista e socialmente reprovável”, mas não determinou a retirada imediata da gravação.


Print de transmissão do influenciador de extrema direita Paulo Figueiredo no YouTube


Para a professora do Grupo de Estudos e Pesquisas em Psicodinâmica do Trabalho Feminino (Psitrafem) da Universidade de Brasília (UnB) Carla Antloga,

o discurso contrário ao voto feminino e outras “manifestações misóginas” não são casos isolados, mas representam a “reativação de argumentos históricos que defendiam a exclusão das mulheres da vida política”.


Nesse contexto, conforme relatou, falas como as de Paulo Figueiredo funcionam como uma tentativa de silenciar mulheres que ocupam espaços públicos e políticos. “A pesquisadora Rita Segato vai chamar isso de ‘pedagogia da crueldade’”, disse Antloga. “[É] o uso da violência sexual verbalizada como piada que termina cumprindo uma função de ensinar para todas as mulheres que, se elas ocuparem a cena política, se falarem ou se manifestarem, [o ataque] também pode acontecer com elas. Por isso, [o termo] ‘pedagógica’, usado no sentido de ensinar por meio da crueldade”, explicou.


A professora ressalta que a violência contra a mulher utilizada como linguagem política não é um evento exclusivamente brasileiro. Para ela,

o fenômeno está relacionado a uma “articulação internacional entre …

author: Unknown
title: Kalkan: Everyone should approach the process with sensitivity
content:
Duran Kalkan, a member of the Abdullah Öcalan Social Sciences Academy, made important assessments of current developments during a special program broadcast on Medya Haber television.


We publish excerpts of the interview. 


The Follow-up and Evaluation Commission held its first meeting. This was seen as an important development, but we also see that there have been provocations, and Leader Apo has also made assessments on this issue recently.


First of all, I respectfully salute Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan]. Yes, today Leader Apo made a statement regarding the process, and the President of Turkey also made assessments and expressed views on the process in clearer and more definitive terms. What we see is that the parties are more determined and clearer in advancing the process. This was clearly expressed both in the statement from the Turkish Presidency and in Leader Apo’s statement. That is certain, first of all. Of course, an important aspect of the statements was that they contained a warning in the face of the provocative attempts of those opposed to the process. They made clear that no provocation could constitute an obstacle to the development of the process and that the Peace and Democratic Society Process would be successfully carried forward and advanced. This is quite important and clear.


This also shows that there are attacks coming from many fronts. In particular, there is opposition to the process from rent-seeking circles, racist circles, and, how shall I put it, some very arrogant and delusional circles. But some racist and rent-seeking circles have become much more aggressive recently.


They are attempting to sabotage the process by staging various fabricated schemes, wondering whether they might somehow derail it. Of course, this has existed from the beginning. But it appears to have increased somewhat recently. What does this indicate? It means there is development in the process, there is progress, and there is greater determination. If this were not the case, if the process were not moving forward and there was no progress, there would obviously be no need for so many attacks. There would not be such multifaceted attacks coming from so many fronts. The existence of these provocations clearly demonstrates the progress being made in the process.


In short, the process is moving forward, and it has accelerated recently. We know that with the law referred to as the framework law, which passed parliament on the night of August 10, the process actually entered its second phase as well—the phase of developing its legal and political dimensions. For the first time, a legal step was taken. Of course, many democratic circles responded to it with criticism. The Kurdish side also criticized its shortcomings, mistakes, narrow scope, lack of inclusiveness, and language. But at the same time, it strongly embraced its historical significance and importance.


This was Leader Apo’s position from the outset. He assessed that the law had at least temporarily stopped the war and opened the way for the parties to engage in politics, creating an opportunity to do so. He considered this highly important. Freeing a century-old, grave problem such as democratization and the Kurdish question—a whole complex of problems shaped entirely around violence—from this framework, opening the way for politics in these matters, and making it possible to seek solutions to problems through political means is no simple matter. Leader Apo described this as moving “from the gallows to the table.” The situation was that important and serious, both in terms of the Kurdish question and democratization. Of course, shortcomings can be criticized; that is a separate matter. But its historical significance was on this level.


Within this framework, new steps are also being taken. The body responsible for carrying out the process outlined by the law held its first meeting as of August 24. This is another important step.


Our basic criteria


It is clear that there is determination. There has also been some acceleration, particularly on the part of the state and government, which are now taking steps more quickly. The public has been informed that four subcommissions have been established, and their members have been named. What is their framework? Who will they consist of? How will they work? These things are not clear and have not been sufficiently explained to the public. They will undoubtedly be explained in due course, and we hope …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Critical minerals policy framework linked to Pax Silica?
content:
“The presidential order is apparently intended to assure potential investors that national government mechanisms are in place to respond to Pax Silica’s mineral requirements.”


CAGAYAN DE ORO — Concerned groups expressed alarm following the issuance of an executive order establishing a policy framework for developing the critical minerals industry.


The International League of Peoples’ Struggles (ILPS) Philippines and the Legal Rights and Natural Resources Center (LRC) suspected that Executive Order (EO) No. 122 issued by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on August 18 is linked to the United States (U.S.)-led

Pax Silica initiative

 that aims to establish a 1,600-hectare industrial hub in New Clark City in Tarlac.


The site is being promoted as an economic security zone that would strengthen shared supply chains in critical minerals, semiconductors, electronics, and other goods.


Arnold Padilla, ILPS Philippines secretary-general, said that the order’s issuance happened ahead of the upcoming Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) Investors Forum in September. “The presidential order is apparently intended to assure potential investors that national government mechanisms are in place to respond to Pax Silica’s mineral requirements.”


The industrial hub under Pax Silica is set to be built within the LEC. 


Exploration


Under the EO, a national exploration and mineral reservation program is set to be implemented by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) of the Department of the Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). The program aims to identify and evaluate new critical mineral deposits. 


Critical minerals, under the order, refers to “essential inputs for clean energy transition technologies, advanced manufacturing, digital infrastructure, national defense, and other strategic industries necessary to promote industrialization, energy security, economic resilience, and sustainable development.”


There is also a strict implementation of the “Use it or Lose it” policy, directing the DENR to enforce the timely and responsible development of critical mineral mining tenements. Those tenements that are found to be in material non-compliance without valid justification shall be subject to cancellation.


Moreover, areas covered by cancelled, expired, relinquished, surrendered, or freed-up critical mining tenements may be considered as critical mineral reservations, subject to verification and assessment.


In coordination with DENR-MGB and other concerned government agencies, the Privatization and Management Office is also directed “to accelerate the disposition and privatization of all government-owned critical mineral mining assets.”


The order also directed the reorganization of the Mining Industry Coordinating Council (MICC) and streamlining and digitalizing the mining permitting process through a virtual one-stop shop.


Suspicions


In a statement, lawyer Mai Taqueban, LRC executive director, expressed concern about the inclusion of critical minerals for advanced manufacturing, digital infrastructure, and national defense in implementing a national exploration and mineral reservation program.


“This squarely frames our critical minerals policy within the Pax Silica framework, and confirms suspicions of the intent to link domestic mining and minerals processing to the ‘war production’ value chain,” she said.


Read:


‘Pax Silica’ initiative seen as war production, environment destruction


She stressed that the EO opens up nine million hectares of potential areas having mineral deposits, as reported by the Philippine Board of Investments, to mining exploration and reservation. “This represents a potential 1,000% increase of mining land area compared to the present total hectarage of approved mining projects.”


More than 790,000 hectares of land in the country are covered by large-scale mining contracts, according to Acting Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna.


On February 4, the Philippine government and the U.S. signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to diversify global critical mineral supply chains. The partnership reportedly provides a framework to have stable and resilient supply and value chains in critical minerals and rare earths in both countries.


ILPS Philippines maintained that the Pax Silica initiative, including the new order of Marcos Jr., only serves the interest of the U.S. and not the interest of the Filipino people.

(DAA)

author: Brian Hioe
title: Recent Controversies About Energy in Taiwan Touch on Indigenous Energy Poverty, Industrial Users
content:
A STUDY BY National Taiwan University recently showed that Indigenous households are disproportionately impacted by energy poverty. Energy poverty is a term defined by using more than 10% of one’s income on electricity fees.

The study found that energy poverty affects 52.2% of disadvantaged households in designated Indigenous areas, while energy poverty affects 42.9% of disadvantaged households in Han majority areas. Likewise, 57.3% of households surveyed reported being unable to pay power bills at least once, while 2.9% had power cut off. 32.4% of those surveyed who had air conditioning struggled to pay for its use, while 37% could not afford replacing their current air conditioning unit. 42% were unaware of programs to partially subsidize the replacement of outdated power-wasting appliances, while 10.2% were aware of such subsidies but still could not afford replacing air conditioning units with them.

The study was conducted by surveying 578 disadvantaged Indigenous households. The survey’s findings were framed by researchers at National Taiwan University’s Risk Society and Policy Research Center as showing the persistence of “green colonialism” in Taiwan.

Earlier this month, Greenpeace Taiwan criticized new draft amendments to the Energy Administration Act, which would exempt energy users who had a new or recently expanded energy contract from being required to install self-use power generation equipment or energy storage equipment. The draft bill, which was passed by the Economics Committee of the legislature, differed from the Executive Yuan’s version of the bill, which would have required electricity users who reach a certain level of energy consumption to install such equipment.

In particular, the bill has been criticized as letting Taiwan’s 400 heavy energy users off the hook. Such heavy energy users constitute more than 40% of Taiwan’s energy use. As such, it is thought that such energy users may expand contracts to avoid falling under this requirement, or that they may take advantage of the five-year grace period that the legislation allows for.

Greenpeace Taiwan has, consequently, called for the bill to be returned to committee review and suggested that the legislature was simply following what the Chinese National Federation of Industries had wished for. The Federation had previously called for expanded contracts to be exempt from such regulations.

Contention about energy in Taiwan is expected to continue, then. The government has long had priorities on trying to please industrial users, at the expense of regular citizens, and this may be another case in point.

author: rti_admin
title: India’s Unfinished Independence
content:
Every August 15, the flag goes up over the Red Fort, the anthem plays in every school and University for a day to celebrate being free. We call it Independence Day — the day India stopped being ruled by the British after two hundred years. And I celebrate it too. But every year, sitting with it a little longer than a headline or a holiday usually gets, one question won’t leave me. Free from what, exactly, and free for whom? The British extracted our wealth, silenced us, and treated us like subjects and inhumane instead of people. They eventually left. But did the thing they left behind actually go with them? Seventy-five-plus years later, many people are still living under a kind of threat, inhuman, and subject to no major change, and the political power is transferred from one hand to another. That time, foreign rule, and the present time, the elite and the oppressed class. caste, patriarchy, or social hierarchy systems- nobody ever really dismantled them, just handed them down like inheritance. The face in charge changed. For too many people, the situation underneath it didn’t. None of this is me rejecting the freedom we won or the people who died for it. It’s me refusing to let “freedom” become something we wave on a flagpole once a year without looking at who still doesn’t have it. After independence, many have hope for major change. We are ruling ourselves at least; nobody discriminates against us, but it is only theoretical, not practical.

We, the people of India, aren’t one religion. We’re not just Hindu, or just Muslim, or Christian, or Sikh — and the Constitution doesn’t lean on any of that in its opening line. It says: “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.” That’s a bigger sentence than it looks. India was never built to belong to one group. Many people are sacrificing their lives, their homes, their hope, their relatives, etc., every family, every tongue, every tradition, without asking anyone to give up who they are to be let in. The Constitution doesn’t just govern us. It protects the different ways we live, our culture, tradition, and language. But that raises a fair question: why does a free people need a document telling them how to live? If human beings are born free, shouldn’t that be enough on its own? For most of history, freedom on paper and freedom in real life were two completely different things. Before the Constitution, millions of people on this land weren’t fully recognized as human, and they were denied all human rights. No education, no right to object to injustice out loud, no fundamental rights. treated as animals; they were not counted as citizens. Two hundred years of British rule made all of that worse, and many people gave everything to end it. Even now, it’s worth asking: is that independence something everyone actually gets to feel, or is it still a promise some people are still waiting on? The Ambedkar Constitution is not just a rulebook. They wrote down a vision; it is a way of life, what Ambedkar called Prabuddha Bharat, an “Enlightened India” where every person could live with dignity and respect, no exceptions. A constitution isn’t a book or a scripture. It’s that imagination of a glorious society, made enforceable.

When Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and the others wrote the Constitution, they weren’t just setting up a government. They were imagining a civilization. Ambedkar called it Prabuddha Bharat — an Enlightened India — where a person’s caste, gender, religion, or birth wouldn’t determine how freely they could move, speak, or live. Liberty, equality, and fraternity weren’t supposed to just sit in the preamble looking nice. They were supposed to be alive. On the eve of the Constitution’s adoption, Ambedkar warned that India was walking into a life full of contradictions — political equality on paper, and deep social and economic inequality in daily life. He said if that contradiction were allowed to go unaddressed, the people suffering under it would eventually blow up the whole structure of political democracy. That warning is still hanging over us, mostly ignored. Caste wasn’t invented by the British — it existed long before them, and it outlived them too. Dalits and Adivasis still face discrimination in villages, in workplaces, in schools, and even in death — separate cremation grounds, separate wells, and separate seating still exist in parts of this country. People still get attacked over things as small as riding a horse to their own wedding, wearing certain …

author: Mavic Conde
title: Cantilan LGU issues pro-mining resolution despite residents’ opposition
content:
A 2018 photo of MMDC’s mining site in Barangay Cabangahan in Cantilan town. Contributed photo.

CANTILAN, Surigao del Sur – This town’s local government approved a “resolution of no objection” to a mining firm’s application for a special tree-cutting and earth-balling permit just five days after residents rejected the proposal at a public hearing.

Dated July 27, 2026, the resolution stated that the Sangguniang Bayan found it appropriate to grant the request, provided that Marcventures Mining and Development Corporation (MMDC) secures all required permits and clearances before beginning work.

The resolution is required for MMDC to apply for a permit from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), covering the cutting of trees across 47.10 hectares in barangay Cabangahan in preparation for its 2027 mining operations.

Following an endorsement from Mayor Philip Pichay’s office, environment committee chair Jimbo Luarez moved for its approval which was unanimously seconded by the Sanggunian members.

In a virtual interview, Cantilan Water District Vicente Chair Cirilo Iriberri called the decision disappointing, stressing that the public hearing appeared to have been held merely for compliance.

The Water District opposed the resolution and campaigned for the protection of the Carac-an watershed, a critical source of clean water for the municipality. MMDC also operates within the watershed.

Iriberrii said that cutting hectares of trees can dry up water sources and worsen flooding. “During the rainy season turbidity levels can shoot up to 1,000 Nephelometric Turbidity Units, far beyond our 500 limit. We have no choice but to wait for it to subside.”

In a statement, the Cantilan Water District warned that the ongoing threats of El Niño must be a concern among the Sangguniang members.

The resolution recognizes the need to protect water sources through prohibiting tree-cutting and earth-balling within 20 meters of either side of any body of water within or adjacent to the project area. However, it does not mention the watershed’s designation as a critical forest reserve or that MMDC’s permit expires in 2027.

Bulatlat reached out to Vice Mayor Rodrigo Eleazar who presided over the public hearing through his official Facebook account but he has not yet replied.

Raymond Ambray, head of the ecology desk of the Diocese of Tandag, said that the province should prioritize agriculture, with rice farming and fishing as remaining key sources of livelihood. While he recognizes mining’s economic contributions, he said that it should not come at the expense of food security and environmental protection.

Cantilan is considered the province’s rice?producing town. For resident and retired forester Agustin Andoy who witnessed how rice fields near their house turned red with silt, the contradiction is hard to reconcile. “Legality feels meaningless, especially when it legitimizes the destruction of the environment and only few benefits.”

During a June 23 municipality session, an MMDC representative acknowledged that of the 600 hectares disturbed by its mining operations, only 200 hectares were rehabilitated. (RTS, DAA)

title: How the Media Sells Genocide
content:
Western media, by employing double standards, censorship, deceptive language, amplifying Israeli lies and dehumanizing Palestinians, facilitates the genocide in Gaza.


 


CHRIS HEDGES


Aug 24, 2026


 


The Western media manufactures consent for genocide. It normalizes Israel’s decades-long military 

occupation

 and 

apartheid

. It erases Israel’s flagrant 

violations

 of international law. It perpetuates the fallacy of Israeli victimhood. It 

betrays

, discredits and demonizes the work of Palestinian journalists and media workers in Gaza, at least 220 of whom have been 

killed

 by Israel between Oct. 7, 2023, and August 2025. It supinely 

accepts

 draconian Israeli censorship. It acquiesces with tepid letters of protest at Israel’s 

refusal

 to allow foreign reporters in Gaza — an effort by Israel to mask its 

war crimes

. It 

amplifies

 Israeli lies, from 

beheaded babies

 to widespread 

sexual assault

 of Israeli women on Oct. 7, to obfuscate the truth.


 


When writing about Gaza, verbs are in the 

passive

 tense. There is no subject. No one is accountable. 

Genocide

, it seems, is an act of God. No different from an earthquake or tsunami. Clichés and opaque adjectives such as the “cycle of violence” or “clashes” distort and falsify reality.


 


“If thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought,” George Orwell 

warned

.


 


Terms such as “genocide,” “atrocity,” “ethnic cleansing” and “occupied territories” magically disappear from media reports on Palestinians, whose resistance is routinely 

described

 as “savage” and “barbaric.” New York Times reporters are 

instructed

 by editors to avoid terms such as “Palestine,” “genocide,” “carnage,” “refugee camp,” “slaughter” and “massacre,” when referencing Palestinians.


 


The media slavishly regurgitates what Israel feeds it. Saturation bombing 

becomes

 

“surgical air strikes.” Israel’s weaponization of famine 

becomes

 a “food shortage.” The 

killing

 of unarmed civilians — including children — becomes “clashes.” The hilltop fortress-like compounds of Jewish colonists 

becomes

 

“neighborhoods.” Extrajudicial assassination of a journalist or a doctor 

becomes

 “died.”


 


Genocide, 

referred

 to as the “Israel-Hamas war” is 

justified

 as “self-defense,” part of the mantra of Israel’s “right to defend itself.” When schools, hospitals, clinics, ambulances, mosques, churches and other civilian targets are obliterated, they are 

labeled

 “Hamas command centers” or targeted because Hamas is “

using

 civilians as human shields” — something Israel does 

routinely

, when the army binds detained Palestinians and forces them to enter potentially booby-trapped 

buildings

 and 

tunnels

 ahead of Israeli troops.


 


When Israelis are held by Hamas, they are “

hostages

,” even if they 

serve

 in the military. When Palestinians — 

including

 

children — are held without charges or trial and disappeared into Israeli detention centers, where torture is “

widespread

” and “

systematic

,” they are “

prisoners

.”


 


Missile attacks on 

tent cities

 or hospitals are blamed on Palestinian armed groups firing errant rockets. If Israel acknowledges the attacks — which very rarely happens — they are described as a “tragic mistake.”


 


Civil institutions in Gaza are 

characterized

 as “Hamas-run” to cast doubt on the veracity of what they report. The New York Times routinely 

qualifies

 announcements from the Gaza Health Ministry by noting it “does not distinguish between civilians and combatants,” masking the slaughter of tens of thousands of civilians.


 


The result is some of the most convoluted writing in the history of journalism, 

including

 

the Nov. 5, 2023 New York Times headline that reads: “Explosions Gazans Say Was Airstrike Leaves Many Casualties in Dense Neighborhood.”


 


“When Middle East Eye journalists

 

Mohamed Salama

 and 

Ahmed Abu Aziz

, along with Reuters photojournalist 

Hussam al-Masri

, and freelancers 

Moaz Abu Taha

, and 

Mariam Dagga

 — who had worked with several media outlets, including the Associated Press — were 

killed

 in a “double tap” strike — designed to kill first responders arriving to treat casualties from initial strikes — at Nasser Medical Complex, how did Western news agencies respond?” I asked in my column 

The Betrayal of Palestinian Journalists

.


 


“Israeli military says strikes on Gaza hospital targeted …

title: FEDA takes over Freedom Vigil for Abdullah Öcalan
content:
The Democratic Alevi Federation in Europe (FEDA), based in France, has taken over the Freedom Vigil in Strasbourg, home to the institutions of the Council of Europe, in its 739th week.


The vigil, which has continued uninterrupted since June 2012, has been maintained since Sunday by FEDA Co-chair Şahin Polat and FEDA members Daimi Gören, Eylem Çiçek, Veli Tekiner and Sidar Içli.


 


FEDA Co-chair Şahin Polat said on behalf of the group that the vigil represents an ongoing struggle against the stance of European states on the Kurdish question following Abdullah Öcalan’s handover to Turkey in 1999.


Polat said FEDA members had volunteered to take part in the vigil and regarded supporting the action as a responsibility, particularly at a time when efforts are underway to implement Abdullah Öcalan’s “Call for Peace and a Democratic Society.”


We see peace as a responsibility we must fulfil


Polat stressed the importance of the struggle for peace for Alevis and said: “Just as deeply as we mourn the lives we have lost, those who have fallen, we see working for peace as a responsibility we must fulfil.”


Polat said they had taken over the vigil for one week to support Abdullah Öcalan’s call. He added: “We are here to respond to Mr. Öcalan’s call for peace, conscious that we Alevis will be among those who benefit most from peace. We are here to once again lend our voice and support to the Call for Peace and a Democratic Society, and to demand Mr. Öcalan’s freedom and his right to hope.”


Polat said, “We are actors for peace and a safeguard of democratic society, and we stand behind Mr. Öcalan’s call for peace.”


FEDA Co-chair Polat also reiterated from Strasbourg the demand for the freedom of all political prisoners, alongside Abdullah Öcalan.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: UPLB decries systematic red-tagging of constituents
content:
“The government must be held accountable for continuing to fund and sustain avenues that manufacture malicious narratives.”


By Jian Martin Tenorio

Bulatlat.com


LOS BAÑOS, Laguna — A Facebook page misusing the name of the official student publication of the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) continues to red-tag campus journalists, youth organizations, and university officials, prompting wide condemnation and calls for academic and press freedom.


In a

statement

 jointly released on August 26, the UPLB Office of the Chancellor, University Student Council (USC), and

UPLB Perspective

 denounced the attacks.


Created on April 4, he Facebook page continues to post photos and videos explicitly tagging UPLB student formations as sites for underground recruitment and insurgent activities while university officials are labeled as enablers.


Citing the landmark Supreme Court ruling

Deduro vs. Vinoya

 (G.R. No. 254753), the statement decried the ongoing attacks as calculated acts meant to threaten UPLB constituents and their civic rights.


“Critical discourse, lawful assembly, campus journalism, and community advocacy are protected democratic rights. We categorically reject any attempt to criminalize student activism and independent campus press work,” the statement read.


UPLB also affirmed its role as a “safe haven” where community members are free to engage in societal critique and “progressive nation-building.”


On March 22, 2021, UPLB officials and sectoral groups signed the

Safe Haven Resolution

 which upholds free critical thinking on campus. Student groups have long called for its stronger implementation as red-tagging against student council members and activists persists.


Attack on campus press 


UP Solidaridad, the UP System-wide alliance of student publications of which UPLB Perspective is a member, also condemned the deliberate attacks on press freedom.


In its August 25

statement

, UP Solidaridad cited the

investigation

 of the Digital Forensic Research Lab (DFRLab) in June 2026 which included “UPLB Perspective Exposed” as among the Facebook pages systematically red-tagging student formations and progressive organizations.


The alliance also called for government accountability for the persistent red-tagging of campus journalists which targets their right to freely “report, investigate, criticize, and hold institutions and those in power accountable.”


“The government must be held accountable for continuing to fund and sustain avenues that manufacture malicious narratives. Instead of protecting students and upholding their rights, the state enables campaigns that criminalize legitimate dissent, and expose them to different forms of state repression,” the statement read.


‘Chilling effect’


For Carl Mhel Tabora, editor-in-chief of

UPLB Perspective

 and one of those targeted by the Facebook page, the red-tagging posts are intended to create a “chilling effect” on campus journalists and those who plan to join the publication.


According to Tabora, “UPLB Perspective Exposed” altered their promotional materials for their apprenticeship process using artificial intelligence (AI), discouraging participation and engagement with the student publication.


“The red-tagging will have a certain chilling effect to the people who see it and on how

UPLB Perspective

 is perceived by the public because of those baseless accusations against the publication,” Tabora said.


Tabora also noticed how the red-tagging posts are shared to Facebook groups with thousands of members, including those intended for police officers and military reservists, putting their reporters at risk.


He stressed that this is not the first time

UPLB Perspective

 was targeted by the same tactic, as a defunct Facebook page bearing the name “UPLB Perspective True Colors” also published similar content targeting the publication and those who engage with it.


Despite the persistent threats, he said that

UPLB Perspective

 will remain steadfast in fulfilling its duty as a student publication.


“We affirmed in the editorial board that red-tagging will never be a reason for UPLB Perspective to abandon its duty to serve the people. At the same time, it only gives us more reason to intensify our pro-people journalism,” Tabora said.

(RTS, DAA)

UPLB decries systematic red-tagging of constituents

author: Brian Hioe
title: Removal of “Chainsmoker Cat” Shows When Government Violates Free Speech in the Name of Anti-Drug Policies
content:
AN INVESTIGATION LAUNCHED by the Health Promotion Administration has resulted in the removal of the anime Chainsmoker Cat from streaming platform Bahamut Animation Crazy. This occurred after complaints by the John Tung Foundation, the Taiwan Anti-Smoking Alliance, and other groups that the anime promoted smoking.

In particular, Bahamut Animation Crazy removed the anime before the investigation was complete. No investigation report or removal order had yet been issued. Other streaming platforms have done similarly with the show.

As such, animation groups such as the ACGN Creative Rights Association have protested an act they view as potentially having a widespread chilling effect. The investigation could have resulted in fines of up to 1 million NT.

Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang has stated that the show did not obscure tobacco brands or contain warnings about the dangers of tobacco during scenes of smoking, which is required under the Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act.

Nevertheless, the show already contains disclaimers about the dangers of excess drinking and smoking. Likewise, the show’s plot generally follows the zany and humiliating antics of the main character because of their debilitating nicotine addiction. It is hard to think that the show is a positive depiction of smoking.

The ACGN Creative Rights Association has further criticized that the anime was broadcast in a late-night time slot and has a PG-15 rating, meaning that the intended target audience was not children, but rather adult men. The organization has cited that the actions of authorities violate the principle of proportionality and continue the pattern of forcing platforms to take the risk of legal fines, again reinforcing a chilling effect when it comes to possible fines.

Although Chainsmoker Cat is a Japanese anime, it is still required to comply with domestic regulations. Apart from the difficulty of that when it comes to foreign media, one notes that the National Communications Commission is currently non-functional, due to budget cuts and a refusal to appoint new members to it by the KMT.

Still, one notes that this is not the first time that authorities have been willing to trample on free speech in the interests of what is framed as anti-drug policy. The Taiwanese government previously suggested that it might pursue cannabis decriminalization advocates, such as former Green Party chair and human rights lawyer Zoe Lee, with the view that advocating for decriminalization constituted incitement to drug use. The Ministry of Justice also suggested that it might pursue depictions of cannabis usage in the media, such as by artists or in music videos, on the grounds that this is inciting cannabis usage. In response, to highlight the absurdity of the act, Lee filed a criminal case against Elon Musk, a well-known proponent of cannabis.

It can be expected that the Taiwanese government will continue to be draconian on the matter of drug decriminalization. Nevertheless, when there remain many smokers in Taiwanese society, it is surprising to see the government take such a strong stance against depictions of smoking, even less than positive ones.

author: rti_admin
title: The Vanishing Government School: Caste, Class, and the Quiet Dismantling of India’s Public Education Promise
content:
“The debate over school closures is not about infrastructure alone. It is about deciding whose children deserve a neighbourhood school and whose education can be sacrificed in the name of efficiency and reform.”

Abstract: Over the past decade, India has witnessed the closure or merger of more than 93,000 government schools—a transformation officially justified as administrative “rationalisation” and educational efficiency. Yet this process is unfolding unevenly, with its greatest consequences borne by Dalit, Adivasi, OBC, and poor Muslim children, who rely overwhelmingly on neighbourhood government schools. Drawing upon the latest NITI Aayog report, UDISE+ data, parliamentary records, constitutional provisions, and recent field reporting, this article argues that school consolidation is not merely a technical reform but a restructuring of educational access with profound implications for social justice. It contends that the shrinking of public schooling undermines the constitutional promise of equality and revives an older hierarchy in which quality education increasingly becomes the privilege of those who can afford it, while the marginalised are left to negotiate longer distances, greater exclusion, and diminished educational opportunity.

On 17 June 2026, officials in Uttar Pradesh’s Gorakhpur district issued a routine administrative order directing the merger of Primary School Mirza Babu with another government school located several kilometres away. Similar directives soon appeared across Mathura and other districts, instructing authorities to identify schools with fewer than twenty students for consolidation.

Such notifications rarely attract national attention. They are framed as bureaucratic necessities intended to optimise resources and improve educational quality. Yet behind these seemingly ordinary administrative decisions lies one of the most significant transformations of India’s public education system since Independence.

According to information placed before Parliament, the number of government schools declined from 11.07 lakh in 2014–15 to nearly 10.13 lakh in 2024–25, representing a loss of more than 93,000 schools over a decade. The scale is staggering: approximately twenty-five government schools disappeared every day for ten consecutive years. Simultaneously, the share of children studying in government schools has steadily declined while enrolment in private institutions has continued to expand. These trends are documented not only in parliamentary records but also in the NITI Aayog’s 2026 report, School Education System in India: Temporal Analysis and Policy Roadmap for Quality Enhancement, which presents perhaps the most comprehensive recent assessment of India’s schooling landscape.

The closure of a school, however, cannot be understood merely as the disappearance of a building. For millions of children belonging to Dalit, Adivasi, OBC, and economically disadvantaged Muslim communities, the neighbourhood government school represents the first—and often the only—meaningful encounter with the Indian state. It is where constitutional promises of equality, citizenship, and social mobility become tangible. When such institutions disappear, the burden does not fall equally across society. Middle-class families frequently possess alternatives: private schools, transport, digital learning resources, and supplementary coaching. Marginalised households often possess none of these. Consequently, what appears as administrative efficiency in policy documents frequently translates into educational exclusion on the ground.

This article argues that the ongoing wave of government school mergers represents far more than an exercise in administrative rationalisation. It reflects a broader restructuring of India’s public education system that disproportionately disadvantages historically marginalised communities. By analysing recent evidence from UDISE+, the NITI Aayog report, parliamentary debates, and constitutional provisions, the article asks a fundamental question: Who pays the social cost of educational rationalisation? It contends that the answer lies at the intersection of caste, class, geography, and state responsibility.

Public Education and the Unfinished Democratic Project

author: Jian Zharese Joies Sanz
title: State neglects fuel education crisis, student union says
content:
Photo from the Philippine Information Agency.

MANILA—The National Union of Students of the Philippines (NUSP) said that the country’s learning crisis is caused by state neglect and the continuing commercialization of education, not by the suspension of classes during disasters.

NUSP released the statement after EDCOM 2 Executive Director Dr. Karol Mark Yee’s warned that consecutive class suspensions due to inclement weather may deepen the ongoing learning crisis. Yee presented plans to amend Executive Order No. 66, s. 2012, which sets the rules for the cancellation or suspension of classes and government work during typhoons and calamities.

NUSP said that amid disasters and the worsening climate crisis, students and academic personnel’s safety must be prioritized. “Students and teachers must not risk their lives to meet certain metrics based on output rather than holistic development and overall well-being.”

NUSP stressed that the Marcos Jr. administration cannot continue to shift the burden of the learning crisis on students and teachers. “We are not convinced by his sham proclamations that education is his ‘greatest priority’ while billions are slashed from the education budget and poured into projects vulnerable to corruption.”

An article from the Development Aid showed that in the previous year, the Philippine government underfunded the education sector, accounting for only 3.6% of the country’s gross domestic product which is below the Unesco-recommended 4-6%.

According to the Makabayan bloc, the budget for the Department of Education (DepEd) suffers the largest total cut of P44.57 billion, with Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE) cut by P33.7 billion. “This is driven by a crippling 64.22% budget cut, effectively halting the construction of much-needed classrooms. This will leave our students in overcrowded and dilapidated learning environments,” Makabayan said.

The coalition highlighted the allocation of PHP 58.53 billion of the pork budget for the Local Government Support Fund. “This LGU pork will be used at the discretion of local chief executives for ayuda, infrastructure projects, and the purchase of vehicles.”

DevelopmentAid said that around 5,000 schools in the Philippines remain without electricity, and 10,000 are without clean water.

NUSP said that 49 out of 113 SUCs will face budget cuts under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP). Despite the education sector’s proposal for a total budget of Php 976 billion out of the proposed Php 7.2 trillion, the Commission on Higher Education will only receive a budget of Php 34.6 billion, which is already reduced from the initially proposed P47.5 billion.

In a statement, the Central Luzon State University Supreme Student Council (CLSU USSC) said that other than corruption, there is also the university administration’s and local authorities’ slow response to the emergency cancellation of classes. “[This] conversation cannot be separated from the broader issue of accountability in governance. Concerns over the use of public funds, allocation of resources, and decisions that directly affect student welfare must not be treated as matters beyond public scrutiny.”

CLSU experienced flooding due to the onslaught of the Southwest Monsoon in the country for the past few weeks. At the University of Santo Tomas, around 5,000 students were stranded inside their campus as heavy flooding blocked its gates on Aug. 17, following the late cancellation of classes from the Manila LGU.

“Class suspensions do not create the learning crisis. Government neglect does. Chronic underfunding does. Corruption does. The commercialization and privatization of education do,” NUSP said.

The student union demanded that Marcos Jr. be held accountable for exacerbating the systemic roots of the crisis and upholding its responsibility to provide accessible, quality, and safe education for all. (RTS,DAA)

author: Cecilia Judge
title: Victory for rank-and-file ticket in Victorian health union election
content:
A group of rank-and-file unionists have ousted the leadership of the Victorian Allied Health Professionals Association (VAHPA) in a landslide election. The VAHPA Pulse ticket, made up of rank-and-file union activists, gained almost twice the vote of the incumbents, VAHPA Unity, and won all the positions.

The VAHPA Unity team has controlled the union for fourteen years and was backed by significant anonymous donations. By contrast, VAHPA Pulse, which I am part of, relied for our support on conviction and our reputations as experienced and uncompromising delegates and activists. Our victory is the culmination of many years of hard work and solid rank-and-file union activity.

The outgoing leadership took control of VAHPA with the ticket name “Clean Sweep”. Clean Sweep faced off against cronies of former national secretary Kathy Jackson, who was responsible for disgraceful corruption and whose actions gave bosses and anti-unionists ammunition to attack unions. Defeating them was an important victory.

However, after the new leadership stemmed the haemorrhaging of members and rebranded the union from HSU Branch 3 to the Victorian Allied Health Professionals Association to signal the beginning of a new era, there has been little in terms of concrete improvements for allied health workers.

I started working in public health just a few months after Clean Sweep came into office. Coming from the community sector, I was excited at the prospect of better pay and conditions in the health system. Today, members are leaving public health for the community sector for the same reason.

However, it’s not just our pay and conditions that have gone backwards under Clean Sweep. Members have also become increasingly frustrated and angry with the lack of communication and transparency on the part of the leadership, as well as its hostility to rank-and-file activity.

After working on the front lines throughout the pandemic, allied health workers had an enterprise agreement pushed on us in 2022 that contained a pathetic 2 percent pay “rise”. As the cost-of-living crisis intensifies and the workload increases in quantity and complexity, VAHPA members increasingly find themselves unable to remain in the sector, whether for financial reasons or their own mental health, often both.

At the 2023 delegates conference there was hope that the situation facing allied health workers might start to turn around. A new public sector organising team presented its three-year plan to rebuild delegate structures and networks in the lead-up to our next round of bargaining. There seemed to be a willingness to involve members and an understanding of the central role delegates play in not only recruiting members but also helping them become active unionists.

We all left excited. Delegates formed new working groups. In particular, professional reference groups were established to provide a mechanism for different occupational groups within VAHPA to raise their particular issues within the union.  Given VAHPA represents around 50 different professions within the complex health system, this work was vital not only to assist the union organisers to understand the issues on the floor, but also to strengthen our identity and ultimately our industrial confidence. All this work was to help inform our strategy before negotiations began on our next agreement.

These exciting developments were unfortunately short lived. We were told by the union leadership, and directly by the secretary, that this work was undermining and divisive to the union as a whole. Radiation therapists, arguably our most organised profession within the union, had been taking initiative in organising across the state and reaching out to their interstate counterparts to learn from their industrial victories. This was attacked by the leadership, which accused these workers of leaving other professions behind.

The message was clear: the leadership calls the shots.

author: Susan Price
title: DSA’s Ella Teevan: ‘Socialism has broken containment’ in the US
content:
Building on the momentum following Zohran Mamdani’s historic victory last year, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have won several primaries, defeating establishment Democrats in the lead-up to the midterm elections in November.

Green Left’s Isaac Nellist was joined by Ella Teevan, a member of the DSA’s National Political Committee, its highest leadership body, to discuss the midterms, Mamdani’s record and how the DSA can build on its successes to strengthen the fight against President Donald Trump’s far-right agenda. This is the first of a two-part interview. Read part two here.

Teevan is a featured speaker at the upcoming Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane. To book tickets, visit ecosocialism.org.au.

What do the DSA’s recent wins in the Democratic primaries reveal about the political situation in the United States?

I think what it reveals is that socialism has broken containment. It’s really exciting and I think the shift really happened in the past few months.

Chris Rabb won in Philadelphia, DSA candidates swept the primaries in New York City, then Melat Kiros won in Colorado, and it showed the public what we already knew in DSA: that socialism can win everywhere.

It’s a national phenomenon, it's so much bigger than Mamdani, and DSA is being taken seriously as an electoral force both by regular people and also by establishment parties and media.

It turns out that socialist ideas are popular!

We already knew after the Bernie Sanders campaign that people are looking for an alternative to our two major parties — the Democrats and the Republicans.

Trump is starting so many foreign wars and interventions, ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] is literally kidnapping and killing our neighbours and regular people are feeling this crisis of affordability.

Meanwhile, the Democratic Party is rolling overhead, and they are similarly responsible for the genocide in Gaza and the extreme levels of wealth and income inequality.

So, DSA is here and ready to provide not just different ideas, but also organisation and even hope to those people who believe it’s possible that we could live in a different kind of society.

We have a right-wing news network, Fox News, which posts clips that try to paint DSA as scary and extreme by talking about our program, Workers Deserve More. They point to things like healthcare for all, free Palestine, abolish ICE, or changing our voting system to be more democratic … Then you see people in the comments say “Oh, this is what socialism is? I guess I’m a socialist”. So that’s really exciting to see.

Of course, this new power comes with new attacks on DSA. The centrist think tank Third Way plans to spend US$13 million [A$18 million] on opposition research on us.

The New York Times is going back to running hit pieces about how all DSA does is fight itself. That might play to the affluent liberals who read the NYT, but to me, it says that the establishment is scared. So, we are doing something right.

To look ahead, we may have up to seven socialists in Congress, eight if you count Bernie Sanders in the Senate — he’s not technically a DSA member but has done so much to bring people into DSA, starting in 2016.

There are so many possibilities with a true socialist bloc in Congress. It’s worth nothing that we had “The Squad” in 2018 — made up of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC), Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar and Ayanna Pressley — which was more of an informal group that largely became known because of how the media framed it.

We are doing something much more intentional this time, and DSA is much bigger and more like a party. DSA plans to work with these socialists in office to advance the demands of our Workers Deserve More program.

It will be important to work out if we actually want to pass policy, or think we can, given we are still a small bloc. This would have to happen after 2028, if the Democratic Party re-takes Congress and the presidency.

Another option is to play an agitational role, to call out the total inadequacy of the Democratic Party and bring more people into the socialist movement.

As for labour struggles, the biggest event on the horizon is May Day 2028. A couple of years ago, the leadership of the United Auto Workers union proposed that unions align their contracts to all expire on May 1, 2028, and use it to increase workers’ leverage and put a spotlight on labour struggles.

To date, only a few unions have done this, but there is still a …

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: How politicians and CEOs got addicted to profit
content:
Hooked: Inside the murky world of Australia’s gambling industry

. By Quentin Beresford. NewSouth Publishing; 352 pages; $39.99

“Of all the prime ministers I’ve known, and I’ve known all of them since Menzies, Albanese is the most gambling-captured prime minister I’ve ever seen”, Tim Costello is quoted as saying in Quentin Beresford’s 2025 book

Hooked: Inside the murky world of Australia’s gambling industry

.

Detailing the history of the gambling industry and its tight connection with the Australian political class,

Hooked

 provides the case for meaningful gambling reform, something neither major political party is willing to implement.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026, which passed parliament in August, hardly scratches the surface of an industry that includes sport betting, both at TABs and online, pokies, casinos and more.

Australian gambling losses are now at a staggering

$31.5 billion

 per year, and have been consistently rising since records began in the mid-1970s. The new legislation doesn’t ban advertising or inducements (like free bets or text messages). It doesn’t remove poker machines from our communities. And it leaves the casinos free to continue operating.

Despite being deemed “

the strongest ever gambling reforms”

 by Communications Minister Anika Wells’ office, the bill stops short of seriously impacting the companies making mega-profits. Beresford’s book gives insight into why, despite there being overwhelming popular support for gambling reform, both Labor and Liberal governments have never been willing to do it.

The entrance of the poker machine was a major turning point in the history of gambling in Australia. In New South Wales in 1956, pokies were legalised and rugby league clubs were given the sole right to operate them. These clubs, according to one expert quoted in

Hooked

, “‘subordinated their social agenda to economic interests’ and grew wealthy on the back of poker machines”.

These league clubs were often the centre of the community. In the 1960s, the South Sydney Junior Leagues Club had 45,000 members. It offered facilities and activities that were not always available to working-class people, like squash courts, a swimming pool, lounge and library. But it also had 111 poker machines, with more on order.

The profits that came from these poker machines in clubs all across New South Wales became the key source of income for the rugby clubs. Beresford quotes the CEO of South Sydney, who recalled that they became “fat, dumb and happy” on the profits from the machines. By the end of the 1960s, there were 20,000 poker machines across New South Wales. Today, more than

80,000 are operating across the state

. This is an increase in poker machines that is twice the rate of population increase.

The relationship between the sports codes and the gambling industry has continued apace. After the release of Labor MP Peta Murphy’s report “You Win Some, You Lose More” in 2023 following a Senate inquiry, the “heavyweights of free-to-air TV and the football codes went all-out to lobby the Albanese government to prevent an ad ban”. This is because it’s not just sports clubs that rely heavily on a revenue stream from pokies.

The AFL receives at least $30 million from gambling agencies revenue, and the NRL $50 million.


The NRL still has direct relationships with gambling agencies, with half the clubs sponsored by agencies. The revenue they receive is not taxed, as both institutions are not-for-profits. The free-to-air broadcasters get around

11 percent of their

 revenue from gambling ads. This amounts to $150 million from gambling advertising each year. These relationships mean that there are multiple institutions lobbying the government; the broadcasters, the clubs and the gambling companies themselves.

One chapter in Beresford’s book details the way these lobbying efforts helped to destroy attempts at reforming the industry by Andrew Wilkie, an independent MP from Tasmania. Wilkie had struck up an agreement with then-Prime Minister Julia Gillard, who was returned to power in a minority government with support from the Greens and independents. Wilkie’s main interest was the gambling industry, which had sucked huge amounts of money from Tasmanians via poker machines and the Wrest Point casino in Hobart. This was Australia’s first legal casino, approved by a Labor government in 1968 following a referendum.

Wilkie had previously campaigned against Coles …

author: Jessica Abbo
title: The University of Queensland is trying to destroy our student union
content:
This morning at the University of Queensland, hundreds of students protested management’s attacks on our student union. A proposed “transition plan” would result in millions of dollars of students’ money (collected through the Student Services and Amenities Fee) being channelled away from democratically elected student representatives to bureaucrats who answer to the university’s administrators.

This is a huge attack on students’ right to politically organise on campus. Currently, the student union is independent from the university, which gives it the ability to criticise and stand up to the administration when it attacks students. Increasing fees, cutting courses and raising rents on student accommodation are common measures taken by the university to make more money at students’ expense. An independent student union can organise students to oppose attacks like these.

Student unions can also organise campaigns about important political issues students care about, such as supporting Palestine or opposing Pauline Hanson. For example, in 2024, 1,500 students demanded the university cut ties with weapons companies and Israel in a meeting called by the student union. University managers despised this rabble-rousing because it called into question their right to take money from companies facilitating the Gaza genocide. The university views protests like these as harmful to its public image and, therefore, to its ability to do business.

The radical potential of the student union is exactly why the university wants to shut it down. Students standing against injustice and preventing the university from doing whatever it wants is a huge thorn in the side of the university bosses.

Unfortunately, we don’t see the union’s radical potential put into action nearly enough. This is a result of it being dominated by moderate Labor students who want to stay on the good side of management. While students are increasingly squeezed by the cost of living, increasingly indebted to the university and facing a hostile world of far-right maniacs, the union has refused to put up a fight. Years of this passive, moderate leadership have led to the present situation. The university is confident it can get rid of the union because few students even know what it is.

We need to fight to defend the union, but it also needs to be rebuilt into a fighting left-wing body that students know will stand up for them. Today’s protest was the first step in what will be a long campaign to defeat the university’s attacks. Convincing students of the importance of the student union and mobilising them to fight back is the best way the union can defend itself.

author: Owen Marsden-Readford
title: Transportation in Sydney is highway robbery
content:
Sydneysiders pay, on average,

more than 15 percent of their income

 just getting around the city week-to-week. It’s a scam that hits working-class residents hardest.

On one hand, there’s the broken public transport system. According to Deutsche Bank’s

Mapping the World’s Prices

 report

, which compares prices across 69 world cities, Sydney’s public transport is the second most expensive in the world, with residents paying up to $2,600 per year in fares. On top of that, the government pays billions to private companies that provide many of the services. The Greater Sydney Bus contract is worth nearly $8 billion, while a private contractor is being paid nearly $4 billion to operate the Metro. So workers pay twice to fund this corporate gravy train—first with their Opal card and again in taxes to fund the companies that profit from running the services.

Yet while costs have soared, the services have gotten worse. Private companies, for example, operate all bus services in the metro area. But the routes are often disrupted, with reduced services and poorer pay and conditions for drivers. The buses are often crowded, if they even show up. In 2023, the ABC

revealed

 that Sydney’s bus contractors were earning bonuses by cancelling thousands of services to meet “on time” targets. “Ghost buses”—ones scheduled to arrive but never do—are common.

The city’s outer suburbs are the least well-served. A 2024

Bus Industry Taskforce report

 found that 235 bus routes failed to meet “minimum service standards”. Most of the routes are in western Sydney. The report said the government needed to invest $10 billion in the coming decades to fix the network.

It is no better for those driving their cars: Sydneysiders pay more than $1 billion in road tolls annually. The city’s thirteen major toll roads are often unavoidable. Transurban, the main company involved, is one of many corporate leeches growing fat off public assets. Many major Transurban toll roads feature locked-in annual price increases of 4 percent or the rate of inflation (whichever is higher), ensuring continuous price hikes for drivers. ​

The state Labor government introduced a $50-per-week toll cap in the latest budget, but it is inadequate. Drivers still pay up to $2,600 per year so that Transurban shareholders can enrich themselves. The cap also leaves the toll road racket untouched. Rather than ending the flow of money to Transurban, the government simply reimburses motorists after they have paid tolls out of pocket. The whole system is highway robbery.

​The first steps to solving the problems are abolishing road tolls, and bringing public transport back into public hands and making it free. Workers should not have to pay for the “privilege” of getting around our own city.

But these measures should only be the beginning. For decades, the city has been designed to make people dependent on cars. The destruction of Sydney’s extensive tram network in the 1950s was one part of this. But more cars and roads relative to trains and trams made congestion worse as the city expanded. A massive investment in public transport infrastructure is needed to reshape Sydney in the interests of working-class residents.
